subject: Hypothesis testing: framing a null and an alternative, measuring the evidence against the null with a test statistic and a p-value, and reading the result without overclaiming
outOfScope: Standard errors, the central limit theorem, the t-distribution and building confidence intervals (see the Sampling distributions pack); this pack only uses an interval to reach a test's decision

Designing and reading product experiments: randomisation units, metrics, peeking and sequential testing, sample-size and power calculations, and corrections for many metrics (see the A/B testing pack)
Bayesian alternatives to a p-value: posterior probabilities of a hypothesis and Bayes factors (see the Bayesian inference pack)
Tests that compare two or more groups: two-sample and paired t-tests, two proportions and ANOVA (see the Comparing groups pack)
Chi-square tests for counts and tables (see the Categorical data pack)
Multiple-comparison procedures in detail, such as Bonferroni or false discovery rate corrections; this pack treats multiple testing only conceptually
Exact binomial tests, nonparametric tests and tests for a variance or standard deviation, beyond naming them
Probability distributions themselves: the normal, t and binomial distributions and their tables (see the Probability distributions pack)
Mathematical theory of tests: likelihood ratios, most powerful tests and power functions
Tooling: Minitab, R, Python, StatKey and spreadsheet functions

prerequisites.reason: Hypotheses are the two claims a test weighs.
The logic assumes the null and looks for evidence against it.
The statistic measures how far the data sit from the null.
The null distribution is the test statistic's distribution under the null.
A randomization test builds the null distribution by simulation.
The p-value is read from the null distribution.
Misreadings presume the definition.
The decision compares the p-value with the significance level.
Not accepting the null follows from assuming it.
Failing to reject is one outcome of the decision rule.
Critical values are set by the significance level.
The test statistic is compared with the critical values.
The steps include choosing a significance level and deciding.
The steps include finding and interpreting the p-value.
The significance level is the Type I error probability.
A Type II error is failing to reject a false null.
The trade-off is between the two errors.
Power is one minus the Type II error probability.
A two-sided p-value counts both tails.
Switching sides after the data inflates Type I errors.
The interval matches a two-sided test.
The proportion test follows the steps.
The p-value depends on the alternative's direction.
The mean test follows the steps.
The mean test proceeds like the proportion test.
Choosing z or t needs the t-test first.
A p-value does not measure importance.
Small samples have low power.
The small sample caution mirrors the large sample one.
Many tests make at least one Type I error likely.
